content: Cefamandole is classified as a second-generation, broad-spectrum cephalosporin antibiotic. The clinically utilized form of cefamandole is cefamandole nafate, which is a prodrug administered parenterally. However, cefamandole is no longer available for use in the United States. Cefamandole exhibits a broad spectrum of antibacterial activity and is effective in treating infections of the skin, bones, joints, urinary tract, and lower respiratory tract. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) data for cefamandole against certain clinically significant microorganisms is reported to be 5 μg/mL. The chemical structure of cefamandole includes an N-methylthiotetrazole (NMTT or 1-MTT) side chain, which is also present in several other cephalosporins. During the metabolic breakdown of cefamandole in the body, free NMTT is released. This can lead to hypoprothrombinemia, likely due to the inhibition of the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase. To mitigate this risk, vitamin K supplementation is recommended during therapy. Additionally, the release of NMTT can cause a disulfiram-like reaction with ethanol, attributed to the inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase. During the reconstitution of cefamandole and ceftazidime, carbon dioxide (CO2) is generated, which can result in an explosive-like reaction when prepared in a syringe. As a second-generation cephalosporin, cefamandole exerts its antibacterial effects by binding to specific penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) and inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis, ultimately leading to bacterial cell death.
